claim: Cleavage of APP by BACE1/β-secretase initiates the amyloidogenic cascade leading to Amyloid-β (Aβ) production.
source: Cleavage of APP by BACE1/β-secretase initiates the amyloidogenic cascade leading to Amyloid-β (Aβ) production.
evidence: This is established knowledge about APP processing pathways in Alzheimer's disease research.

claim: α-Secretase initiates the non-amyloidogenic pathway preventing Aβ production.
source: α-Secretase initiates the non-amyloidogenic pathway preventing Aβ production.
evidence: This is established knowledge about APP processing pathways.

claim: Several APP mutations cause familial Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Several APP mutations cause familial Alzheimer's disease (AD), while the Icelandic APP mutation near the BACE1-cleavage site protects from sporadic dementia, emphasizing APP's role in dementia pathogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of Alzheimer's disease genetics.

claim: The Icelandic APP mutation near the BACE1-cleavage site protects from sporadic dementia.
source: Several APP mutations cause familial Alzheimer's disease (AD), while the Icelandic APP mutation near the BACE1-cleavage site protects from sporadic dementia, emphasizing APP's role in dementia pathogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research on the Icelandic mutation.

claim: α-Cleavage is favored over β-processing in Appp rats.
source: α-Cleavage is favored over β-processing in Appp rats.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including Western blots and ELISA measurements.

claim: Non-amyloidogenic and amyloidogenic APP metabolites are increased and decreased, respectively, in Appp rats.
source: Consequently, non-amyloidogenic and amyloidogenic APP metabolites are increased and decreased, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing changes in sAPPα, sAPPβ, and Aβ levels in Appp rats.

claim: The reverse APP processing shift occurs in Apps rats compared to Appp rats.
source: The reverse APP processing shift occurs in Apps rats.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing opposite changes in APP metabolites in Apps rats.

claim: Protection from and pathogenesis of dementia depend upon combinatorial and opposite alterations in APP metabolism rather than simply on Aβ levels.
source: These opposite effects on APP β/α-processing suggest that protection from and pathogenesis of dementia depend upon combinatorial and opposite alterations in APP metabolism rather than simply on Aβ levels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing opposite APP processing patterns in protective and pathogenic mutations.

claim: The Icelandic mutation protects from aging-dependent cognitive decline.
source: The Icelandic mutation also protects from aging-dependent cognitive decline, suggesting that similar mechanisms underlie physiological cognitive aging.
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Similar mechanisms underlie physiological cognitive aging and Alzheimer's disease protection.
source: The Icelandic mutation also protects from aging-dependent cognitive decline, suggesting that similar mechanisms underlie physiological cognitive aging.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the protective effects of the Icelandic mutation.

claim: β-processing of APP involves an initial cleavage of the APP ectodomain by β-secretase (BACE1), followed by the cleavage of the resultant β-COOH-terminal fragment (βCTF) by γ-secretase to produce amyloid beta (Aβ) and the APP intracellular domain (AID/AICD).
source: The β-processing of APP involves an initial cleavage of the APP ectodomain by β-secretase (BACE1), followed by the cleavage of the resultant β-COOH-terminal fragment (βCTF) by γ-secretase to produce amyloid beta (Aβ) and the APP intracellular domain (AID/AICD).
evidence: This is established knowledge about APP processing pathways, supported by citations.

claim: In the nonamyloidogenic pathway, APP is first cleaved within the Aβ region sequentially by α- and γ-secretase, which produces a smaller P3 fragment and AID/AICD.
source: Alternatively, in the nonamyloidogenic pathway, APP is first cleaved within the Aβ region sequentially by α- and γ-secretase, which produces a smaller P3 fragment and AID/AICD (Sisodia et al., 2001; Sisodia and St George-Hyslop, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The biological functions of APP and its metabolites affect many important neuronal functions related to AD.
source: The biological functions of APP and its metabolites affect many important neuronal functions, related to AD (Barbagallo et al., 2011; Barbagallo et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2012; Matrone et al., 2011; Matrone et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Not just amyloid beta, but the other APP metabolites and the holoprotein itself have important effects on the neuron.
source: Not just amyloid beta, but the other APP metabolites and the holoprotein itself have important effects on the neuron (Del Prete et al., 2014; Fanutza et al., 2015; Fogel et al., 2014; Gulisano et al., 2019; Matrone et al., 2011; Nikolaev et al., 2009; Passer et al., 2000; Puzzo et al., 2017; Rice et al., 2019; Tambini et al., 2019; Yao et al., 2019; Zott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Mutations that affect APP processing either cause or prevent AD for both early and late-onset AD.
source: Mutations that affect APP processing either cause or prevent AD. This is true for both early and late-onset AD (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The K670N/M671L (Swedish) mutation of the NH2-terminal side of the β-cleavage site of APP increases its β-processing and causes a familial form of AD.
source: For example, the K670N/M671L (Swedish) mutation of the NH2-terminal side of the β-cleavage site of APP increases its β-processing and causes a familial form of AD (Citron et al., 1992; Citron et al., 1994; Johnston et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The A673T (Icelandic or protective) mutation, which is COOH-terminal to the β-site of APP, decreases the affinity of APP for BACE1.
source: The A673T (Icelandic or protective) mutation, which is COOH-terminal to the β-site of APP, decreases the affinity of APP for BACE1, and thereby reduces β-processing and protects against late-onset AD and normal cognitive decline (Jonsson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The A673T mutation reduces β-processing and protects against late-onset AD and normal cognitive decline.
source: The A673T (Icelandic or protective) mutation, which is COOH-terminal to the β-site of APP, decreases the affinity of APP for BACE1, and thereby reduces β-processing and protects against late-onset AD and normal cognitive decline (Jonsson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Late-onset AD can be caused by mutations which block the α-processing of APP.
source: Late-onset AD can also be caused by mutations which block the α-processing of APP (Hartl et al., 2018; Suh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Analysis of transgenic APP models are confounded by the overexpression of APP above physiological levels.
source: Analysis of transgenic APP models, which are extensively used in AD research, are confounded by several factors: the overexpression of APP above physiological levels (Saito et al., 2016), the disruption of genes in the transgene integration sites (Goodwin et al., 2019; Tosh et al., 2017), the use of exogenous promoters, which do not replicate the temporal, cell type-specific or spatial expression of the endogenous gene (Rodgers et al., 2012), and the overproduction of multiple, biologically active APP metabolites.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Transgenic APP models are confounded by the disruption of genes in the transgene integration sites.
source: Analysis of transgenic APP models, which are extensively used in AD research, are confounded by several factors: the overexpression of APP above physiological levels (Saito et al., 2016), the disruption of genes in the transgene integration sites (Goodwin et al., 2019; Tosh et al., 2017), the use of exogenous promoters, which do not replicate the temporal, cell type-specific or spatial expression of the endogenous gene (Rodgers et al., 2012), and the overproduction of multiple, biologically active APP metabolites.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Transgenic APP models use exogenous promoters which do not replicate the temporal, cell type-specific or spatial expression of the endogenous gene.
source: Analysis of transgenic APP models, which are extensively used in AD research, are confounded by several factors: the overexpression of APP above physiological levels (Saito et al., 2016), the disruption of genes in the transgene integration sites (Goodwin et al., 2019; Tosh et al., 2017), the use of exogenous promoters, which do not replicate the temporal, cell type-specific or spatial expression of the endogenous gene (Rodgers et al., 2012), and the overproduction of multiple, biologically active APP metabolites.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A transgenic approach will generate a gain of function model organism rather than mimicking the loss of function effect of protective or pathogenic mutations.
source: A transgenic approach will not mimic this loss of function effect but, on the contrary, it will generate a gain of function model organism (i.e. the opposite of the human process that the organism aims to model).
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of transgenic overexpression.

claim: A knock-in (KI) approach eliminates confounding factors present in transgenic models.
source: A knock-in (KI) approach, in which the mutations of interest are introduced into the endogenous gene locus and in which the endogenous regulatory elements of the gene are left intact, eliminates these confounding factors.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of genetic engineering approaches.

claim: The rat was the organism of choice for most behavioral, memory and cognitive research because physiological processes are similar in rats and humans, and the rat is an intelligent and quick learner.
source: The rat was the organism of choice for most behavioral, memory and cognitive research, which is critical when studying neurodegenerative diseases, because physiological processes are similar in rats and humans, and the rat is an intelligent and quick learner (Deacon, 2006; Foote and Crystal, 2007; Kepecs et al., 2008; Whishaw et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Several procedures important in dementia research are more easily performed in rats as compared to mice due to the larger size of the rat brain.
source: Several procedures that are important in dementia research are more easily performed in rats as compared to mice due to the larger size of the rat brain.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of experimental procedures in neuroscience.

claim: Cannulas and micro-dialysis probes can be accurately directed to individual brain regions in rats, causing less damage and increasing specificity.
source: Cannulas -to administer drugs, biologics, viruses etc.- and micro-dialysis probes –for sampling extracellular brain levels of neurotransmitters, Aβ, soluble tau etc.- can be accurately directed to individual brain regions, causing less damage and increasing specificity.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of experimental procedures in neuroscience.

claim: In vivo brain imaging techniques such as MRI and PET can assess the extent and course of neurodegeneration with better spatial resolution in rats.
source: In vivo brain imaging techniques, such as MRI (Bartelle et al., 2016) and PET (Leuzy et al., 2014; Zimmer et al., 2014a; Zimmer et al., 2014b), can assess the extent and course of neurodegeneration with better spatial resolution in rats.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rats are large enough for convenient in vivo electrophysiological recordings or serial sampling of cerebrospinal fluid for detection of biomarkers.
source: Moreover, rats are large enough for convenient in vivo electrophysiological recordings or serial sampling of cerebrospinal fluid for detection of biomarkers.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of experimental procedures in neuroscience.

claim: Adult human and rat brains express both 3R and 4R tau isoforms.
source: Adult human and rat brains express both 3R and 4R tau isoforms (Hanes et al., 2009): in contrast, adult mouse brains express only 4R tau (McMillan et al., 2008), suggesting that the rat may be a better model organism for dementias with tauopathy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Adult mouse brains express only 4R tau.
source: Adult human and rat brains express both 3R and 4R tau isoforms (Hanes et al., 2009): in contrast, adult mouse brains express only 4R tau (McMillan et al., 2008), suggesting that the rat may be a better model organism for dementias with tauopathy.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The rat may be a better model organism for dementias with tauopathy than the mouse.
source: Adult human and rat brains express both 3R and 4R tau isoforms (Hanes et al., 2009): in contrast, adult mouse brains express only 4R tau (McMillan et al., 2008), suggesting that the rat may be a better model organism for dementias with tauopathy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of tau isoform expression between rats and humans.

claim: Rat and human APP differ by 3 amino acids in the Aβ region.
source: Rat and human APP differ by 3 amino acids in the Aβ region (Figure 1A): since aggregated forms of Aβ are by and large considered the main pathogenic molecule in AD and given that human Aβ may have higher propensity to form toxic Aβ species as compared to rodent Aβ, together with the protective and Swedish mutations we introduced mutations to 'humanize' the rat Aβ sequence.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: Human Aβ may have higher propensity to form toxic Aβ species as compared to rodent Aβ.
source: Rat and human APP differ by 3 amino acids in the Aβ region (Figure 1A): since aggregated forms of Aβ are by and large considered the main pathogenic molecule in AD and given that human Aβ may have higher propensity to form toxic Aβ species as compared to rodent Aβ, together with the protective and Swedish mutations we introduced mutations to 'humanize' the rat Aβ sequence.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The humanizing and protective Icelandic mutations were correctly inserted into the Appp/h genome.
source: The humanizing and protective Icelandic mutations (Figure 1A) were correctly inserted into the Appp/h genome (Figure 1B) and expression of App in Appp/p brains was comparable to that detected in Apph/h brains (Figure 1C, p=0.7576).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of App in Appp/p brains was comparable to that detected in Apph/h brains.
source: The humanizing and protective Icelandic mutations (Figure 1A) were correctly inserted into the Appp/h genome (Figure 1B) and expression of App in Appp/p brains was comparable to that detected in Apph/h brains (Figure 1C, p=0.7576).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: App mRNA levels in Apph/h brains were identical to those observed in WT (Appw/w) Long-Evans rats.
source: We have previously shown that App mRNA levels in Apph/h brains was identical to those observed in WT (Appw/w) Long-Evans rats (Tambini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The introduced humanizing plus protective Icelandic mutations do not alter App mRNA expression.
source: Thus, the introduced humanizing plus protective Icelandic mutations do not alter App mRNA expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RT-PCR data showing comparable App mRNA levels.

claim: Cleavage of APP by β-secretase takes place predominantly in acidic compartments.
source: Cleavage of APP by β-secretase takes place predominantly in acidic compartments: this processing releases a long (595 amino acid long, if referring to the APP695 isoform- the most highly expressed in brain) soluble NH2-terminal APP ectodomain (sAPPβ) and a membrane-bound 99 amino acid long fragment (C99 or βCTF).
evidence: This is established knowledge about APP processing.

claim: β-secretase cleavage releases a long soluble NH2-terminal APP ectodomain (sAPPβ) and a membrane-bound 99 amino acid long fragment (C99 or βCTF).
source: Cleavage of APP by β-secretase takes place predominantly in acidic compartments: this processing releases a long (595 amino acid long, if referring to the APP695 isoform- the most highly expressed in brain) soluble NH2-terminal APP ectodomain (sAPPβ) and a membrane-bound 99 amino acid long fragment (C99 or βCTF).
evidence: This is established knowledge about APP processing.

claim: βCTF is cleaved with lax site specificity by γ-secretase into Aβ peptide and the APP intracellular domain (AICD/AID).
source: βCTF is cleaved with lax site specificity by γ-secretase into Aβ peptide and the APP intracellular domain (AICD/AID).
evidence: This is established knowledge about APP processing.

claim: α-secretase cleaves APP along the secretory pathway or on the plasma membrane.
source: Alternatively, α-secretase cleaves APP along the secretory pathway or on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about APP processing.

claim: α-secretase cleavage occurs within the Aβ sequence to produce soluble APPα (sAPPα) and a COOH-terminal membrane-bound 83 amino acid long fragment (C83 or αCTF).
source: This cleavage occurs within the Aβ sequence to produce soluble APPα (sAPPα) and a COOH-terminal membrane-bound 83 amino acid long fragment (C83 or αCTF).
evidence: This is established knowledge about APP processing.

claim: αCTF can be cleaved by γ-secretase into a 'shorter Aβ' peptide, called P3, and AID.
source: αCTF can be also cleaved by γ-secretase into a 'shorter Aβ' peptide, called P3 (see Figure 3A for a depiction of the major Aβ and P3 species), and AID.
evidence: This is established knowledge about APP processing, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: sAPPα and sAPPβ are stable APP metabolites.
source: sAPPα and sAPPβ are stable APP metabolites (Morales-Corraliza et al., 2009), unlike αCTF and βCTF, which are cleared by γ-secretase and lysosomes (Barbagallo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: αCTF and βCTF are cleared by γ-secretase and lysosomes.
source: sAPPα and sAPPβ are stable APP metabolites (Morales-Corraliza et al., 2009), unlike αCTF and βCTF, which are cleared by γ-secretase and lysosomes (Barbagallo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: sAPPα and sAPPβ are better indicators of the rate of cleavage of APP by either α- or β-secretase, respectively.
source: Thus, sAPPα and sAPPβ are better indicators of the rate of cleavage of APP by either α- or β-secretase, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stability of these metabolites.

claim: In vitro studies have shown that the protective Icelandic mutation reduces the rate of APP processing by β-secretase.
source: As noted above, in vitro studies have shown that the protective Icelandic mutation reduces the rate of APP processing by β-secretase; in addition, a non-significant trend towards an increase in the rate of APP cleavage by α-secretase was also noted (Jonsson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In vitro studies showed a non-significant trend towards an increase in the rate of APP cleavage by α-secretase for the protective Icelandic mutation.
source: As noted above, in vitro studies have shown that the protective Icelandic mutation reduces the rate of APP processing by β-secretase; in addition, a non-significant trend towards an increase in the rate of APP cleavage by α-secretase was also noted (Jonsson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: No plaques were evident in 3 month old Apps/s rats.
source: Young rats were chosen to avoid the confounding effect of amyloid aggregation, though it should be noted that no plaques were evident in 3 month old Apps/s rats (Tambini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Y188 detects APP, βCTF and αCTF in Appw/w, Apph/h, Apps/s and Appp/p brains.
source: Y188 detects APP, βCTF and αCTF in Appw/w, Apph/h, Apps/s and Appp/p brains (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: M3.2 detects APP and βCTF only in Appw/w brains.
source: M3.2 detects APP and βCTF only in Appw/w brains (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 6E10 detected APP and βCTF only in Apph/h, Apps/s and Appp/p rats.
source: On the other hand, 6E10 detected APP and βCTF only in Apph/h, Apps/s and Appp/p rats (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: None of the antibodies Y188, M3.2, and 6E10 gave specific signal in Appδ7/δ7 samples.
source: As expected, none of these antibodies gave specific signal in Appδ7/δ7 samples.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 2.

claim: APPh, APPSw and APPp, the protein products of the Apph, Apps and Appp alleles, contain the humanized Aβ sequence.
source: Thus, APPh, APPSw and APPp, the protein products of the Apph, Apps and Appp alleles, contain the humanized Aβ sequence, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the antibody recognition patterns shown in Western blots.

claim: M3.2 is specific for APP molecules containing the rat Aβ sequence.
source: M3.2 is specific for APP molecules containing the rat Aβ sequence; conversely, 6E10 only recognizes APP molecules containing the human Aβ sequence.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing differential recognition patterns.

claim: 6E10 only recognizes APP molecules containing the human Aβ sequence.
source: M3.2 is specific for APP molecules containing the rat Aβ sequence; conversely, 6E10 only recognizes APP molecules containing the human Aβ sequence.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing differential recognition patterns.

claim: sAPPβ was significantly lower in Appp/p as compared to Apph/h brains.
source: sAPPβ was significantly lower in Appp/p as compared to Apph/h brains (Figure 2D, upper panel: quantification in Figure 2L -P = 0.0014).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and quantification data shown in Figures 2D and 2L.

claim: sAPPα was significantly higher in Appp/p as compared to Apph/h brains.
source: In contrast, sAPPα was significantly higher in Appp/p as compared to Apph/h brains (Figure 2D, lower panel: quantification in Figure 2M -P = 0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and quantification data shown in Figures 2D and 2M.

claim: The APPp mutant expressed by the Appp allele is cleaved more efficiently by α-secretase and less efficiently by β-secretase.
source: These findings support the notion that the APPp mutant expressed by the Appp allele is cleaved more efficiently by α-secretase and less efficiently by β-secretase, just like the human counterpart.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sAPPα and sAPPβ data.

claim: APP levels are unchanged in Appp/p brains compared to Apph/h brains.
source: APP levels are unchanged in Appp/p brains (Figure 2E, APP levels detected by 6E10 -P = 0.4586-, Figure 2F APP levels detected by Y188 -P = 0.9385).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: βCTF levels detected by 6E10 were significantly lower in Appp/p as compared to Apph/h brains.
source: βCTF levels detected by 6E10 were significantly lower in Appp/p as compared to Apph/h brains (Figure 2G, p=0.0484): in contrast quantification of βCTF levels detected by Y188 did not show significant differences between these two genotypes (Figure 2H, p=0.4109).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Quantification of βCTF levels detected by Y188 did not show significant differences between Appp/p and Apph/h brains.
source: βCTF levels detected by 6E10 were significantly lower in Appp/p as compared to Apph/h brains (Figure 2G, p=0.0484): in contrast quantification of βCTF levels detected by Y188 did not show significant differences between these two genotypes (Figure 2H, p=0.4109).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Quantification of βCTF levels in 6E10 blots is more accurate than quantification of βCTF levels in Y188 blots.
source: Quantification of βCTF levels in 6E10 blots, where αCTF is not detected (Figure 2C), is more accurate than quantification of βCTF levels in Y188 blots (Figure 2A), where αCTF, which runs very close to βCTF, is the predominant APP-CTF species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the antibodies and the Western blot patterns.

claim: Levels of αCTF were not significantly different between Appp/p and Apph/h brains.
source: Levels of αCTF, albeit slightly higher in Appp/p rats, where also not significantly different between Appp/p and Apph/h brains (Figure 2I, p=0.3121).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The βCTF-Y188/αCTF ratio was not different in Appp/p and Apph/h samples.
source: While the βCTF-Y188/αCTF ratio was not different in Appp/p and Apph/h samples (Figure 2J, p=0.6681), the βCTF-6E10/αCTF ratio was significantly lower in Appp/p brains (Figure 2K, p=0.0007).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The βCTF-6E10/αCTF ratio was significantly lower in Appp/p brains compared to Apph/h brains.
source: While the βCTF-Y188/αCTF ratio was not different in Appp/p and Apph/h samples (Figure 2J, p=0.6681), the βCTF-6E10/αCTF ratio was significantly lower in Appp/p brains (Figure 2K, p=0.0007).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Aβ40 levels are significantly reduced in Appp/p as compared to Apph/h brains.
source: Finally, we measured Aβ40 peptides (human Aβ40 since our KI rats produce human Aβ species) by ELISA. As shown in Figure 2N, Aβ40 levels are significantly reduced in Appp/p as compared to Apph/h brains (p=0.0003).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2N.

claim: Appp KI rats reproduce the APP metabolic changes caused by the Icelandic protective mutation in humans: reduced rate of APP processing by β-secretase and increased rate of APP cleavage by α-secretase.
source: In summary, the data shown in Figure 2 suggest that our Appp KI rats reproduce the APP metabolic changes caused by the Icelandic protective mutation in humans: that is reduced rate of APP processing by β-secretase and increased rate of APP cleavage by α-secretase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective data from Figure 2.

claim: The WAKO Aβ42 ELISA kit could not reliably measure Aβ42 in Appp/p rats.
source: The WAKO Aβ42 ELISA kit could not reliably measure Aβ42, which is considered the main pathogenic Aβ species in humans, in Appp/p rats (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: 6E10 will only measure Aβ38, Aβ40 and Aβ42.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, 6E10 will only measure Aβ38, Aβ40 and Aβ42; in contrast, 4G8 will detect Aβ38, Aβ40, Aβ42 as well as the corresponding P3 peptides P3-22, P2-24 and P3-26, respectively.
evidence: This is based on the epitope specificity of the antibodies shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 4G8 will detect Aβ38, Aβ40, Aβ42 as well as the corresponding P3 peptides P3-22, P2-24 and P3-26.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, 6E10 will only measure Aβ38, Aβ40 and Aβ42; in contrast, 4G8 will detect Aβ38, Aβ40, Aβ42 as well as the corresponding P3 peptides P3-22, P2-24 and P3-26, respectively.
evidence: This is based on the epitope specificity of the antibodies shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Comparing the signal obtained with the 6E10 and 4G8 kits may yield information concerning levels of both Aβ and P3 peptides.
source: Thus, comparing the signal obtained with the two kits may yield information concerning levels of both Aβ and P3 peptides (Siegel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential specificity of the antibodies, supported by citation.

claim: Both MSD ELISA kits detect a specific signal in Apph/h but not Appδ7/δ7 brain homogenates.
source: To determine specificity of these kits, we tested brain homogenates derived from Appδ7/δ7, in which the Aβ-coding region is out of frame with App due to the 7 base pair deletion and that at any rate results in a hypomorphic allele (Tambini et al., 2019), and Apph/h rats. Both kits detect a specific signal -that is in Apph/h but not Appδ7/δ7 brain homogenates (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA validation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Aβ38+P3-22 and Aβ38 were detectable in a few Apph/h brain homogenates only.
source: Aβ38+P3-22 (F (5, 24)=2.578, p=0.0529) and Aβ38 (F (5, 24)=2.554, p=0.0546) were detectable in a few Apph/h brain homogenates only (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Aβ40+P3-24, Aβ40, Aβ42+P3-26 and Aβ42 peptides were significantly reduced, in a gene-dosage-dependent manner, in Appp/h and Appp/p rats.
source: Aβ40+P3-24 (F (5, 24)=34.30, p<0.0001), Aβ40 (F (5, 24)=43.32, p<0.0001), Aβ42+P3-26 (F (5, 24)=5.062, p=0.0026) and Aβ42 (F (5, 24)=13.76, p<0.0001) peptides were significantly reduced, in a gene-dosage-dependent manner, in Appp/h and Appp/p rats (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: No sex-specific effect on Aβ/P3 peptides production was detected in Appp rats.
source: We did not detect any sex-specific effect on Aβ/P3 peptides production.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The Aβ42+P3-26/Aβ40+P3-24 ratio was unchanged in Appp rats.
source: In addition, while the Aβ42+P3-26/Aβ40+P3-24 ratio was unchanged (F (5, 24)=1.694, p=0.1745), analysis of the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio suggests that the Icelandic protective allele may reduce this ratio (Figures 3E,F (5 and 24)=5.756, p=0.013), which could underlie a protective mechanism prompted by the Icelandic variant.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Icelandic protective allele may reduce the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio.
source: In addition, while the Aβ42+P3-26/Aβ40+P3-24 ratio was unchanged (F (5, 24)=1.694, p=0.1745), analysis of the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio suggests that the Icelandic protective allele may reduce this ratio (Figures 3E,F (5 and 24)=5.756, p=0.013), which could underlie a protective mechanism prompted by the Icelandic variant.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3E, though the authors note more animals are needed.

claim: The significance of the differences among genotypes is higher in 6E10 measurements as compared to 4G8 measurements.
source: Although the significance of the differences among genotypes is higher in 6E10 measurements as compared to 4G8 measurements -this is obviously evident when comparing Aβ42+P3-26 and Aβ42 ELISAs- suggesting that P3 peptides may be increased in Appp/h and Appp/p rats, we cannot draw definitive conclusions concerning levels of P3 and whether these levels are changed in a genotype-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the ELISA data.

claim: P3 peptides may be increased in Appp/h and Appp/p rats.
source: Although the significance of the differences among genotypes is higher in 6E10 measurements as compared to 4G8 measurements -this is obviously evident when comparing Aβ42+P3-26 and Aβ42 ELISAs- suggesting that P3 peptides may be increased in Appp/h and Appp/p rats, we cannot draw definitive conclusions concerning levels of P3 and whether these levels are changed in a genotype-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the difference in significance between 6E10 and 4G8 measurements.

claim: Aβ peptides are consistently reduced in Appp rats using two different detection antibodies.
source: Nevertheless, the finding that Aβ peptides are consistently reduced using two different detection antibodies stresses the significance of the finding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of results across different antibodies.

claim: The reduction of Aβ peptides in Appp rats seen in the 6E10-based ELISA is not due to a reduced affinity of Aβ species carrying the protective Icelandic mutation for 6E10.
source: In addition, they exclude the possibility that the reduction of Aβ peptides in Appp rats seen in the 6E10-based ELISA may be due to a reduced affinity of Aβ species carrying the protective Icelandic mutation, which is adjacent to the 6E10 epitope (Figure 1A), for 6E10.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of results with both 6E10 and 4G8 antibodies.

claim: sAPPα is significantly increased in a gene-dosage-dependent manner in Appp/p rats when data from males and females were pooled.
source: When data from males and females were pooled, we detected a gene-dosage-dependent increase in sAPPα (F (5, 24)=6.725, p=0.0043) and a significant decrease in sAPPβ (F (5, 24)=12.64, p=0.0001) in Appp/p rats (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: sAPPβ is significantly decreased in a gene-dosage-dependent manner in Appp/p rats when data from males and females were pooled.
source: When data from males and females were pooled, we detected a gene-dosage-dependent increase in sAPPα (F (5, 24)=6.725, p=0.0043) and a significant decrease in sAPPβ (F (5, 24)=12.64, p=0.0001) in Appp/p rats (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Total APP levels were not changed in either male or female Appp rats.
source: Total APP levels were not changed in either male or females (Figure 5A, males F (2, 12)=1.756, p=0.2144); females (F (2, 12)=2.367, p=0.1360).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 4A (note: text says Figure 5A but refers to Figure 4A based on context).

claim: Levels of mAPP were not significantly changed in Appp rats.
source: Quantification of mature APP (mAPP), immature APP (imAPP), αCTF and βCTF showed the following: levels of mAPP (males F (2, 12)=1.493, p=0.2635; females F (2, 12)=2.090, p=0.1615, Figure 4C) and imAPP were not significantly changed -except for a reduction in imAPP levels in female Appp/h brains (males F (2, 12)=1.036, p=0.3846; females F (2, 12)=4.180, p=0.0419, Figure 4B), which may or may not be confirmed in further analyses- in animals carrying the protective Icelandic mutation.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: imAPP levels were reduced in female Appp/h brains.
source: Quantification of mature APP (mAPP), immature APP (imAPP), αCTF and βCTF showed the following: levels of mAPP (males F (2, 12)=1.493, p=0.2635; females F (2, 12)=2.090, p=0.1615, Figure 4C) and imAPP were not significantly changed -except for a reduction in imAPP levels in female Appp/h brains (males F (2, 12)=1.036, p=0.3846; females F (2, 12)=4.180, p=0.0419, Figure 4B), which may or may not be confirmed in further analyses- in animals carrying the protective Icelandic mutation.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The mAPP/imAPP ratio was not changed in Appp rats.
source: The mAPP/imAPP ratio was also not changed (Figure 4D, males F (2, 12)=1.406, p=0.2828; females F (2, 12)=2.009, p=0.1768).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: βCTF levels were significantly lower in Appp/p females as compared to Apph/h females.
source: βCTF levels were significantly lower in Appp/p females as compared to Apph/h females (Figure 4E, males F (2, 12)=4.131, p=0.0431; females F (2, 12)=4.873, p=0.0282).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Levels of αCTF were not significantly different in Appp rats.
source: Levels of αCTF, albeit slightly higher in Appp/p rats, were also not significantly different (Figure 4F, males F (2, 12)=3.276, p=0.0732; females F (2, 12)=1.869, p=0.1965).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The βCTF/αCTF ratio was decreased significantly in a gene-dosage dependent manner in both sexes of Appp rats.
source: However, the βCTF/αCTF ratio was decreased significantly in a gene-dosage dependent manner in both sexes (Figure 4G, males F (2, 12)=15.15, p=0.0005; females F (2, 12)=27.27, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The protective Icelandic mutation reduced the rate of APP processing by β-secretase and increased rate of APP cleavage by α-secretase in a gene-dosage dependent manner.
source: Overall, the data suggest that the protective Icelandic mutation reduced the rate of APP processing by β-secretase and increased rate of APP cleavage by α-secretase in a gene-dosage dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective Western blot and ELISA data from Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Apps/s rats show an opposite phenotype to Appp rats: reduced rate of APP processing by α-secretase and increased rate of APP cleavage by β-secretase.
source: We have recently shown that Apps/s rats, that is rats carrying two App alleles with the humanizing and pathogenic Swedish mutations, show an opposite phenotype: that is reduced the rate of APP processing by α-secretase and increased rate of APP cleavage by β-secretase (Tambini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Aβ38+P3-22 levels were not significantly altered by either sex or genotype in Apps rats.
source: While Aβ38+P3-22 levels were not significantly altered by either sex or genotype (Figures 5A,F (5 and 23)=1.779, p=0.1570), Aβ38 (Figures 5A,F (5 and 23)=27.42, p<0.0001), Aβ40+P3-24 (Figures 5B,F (5 and 23)=86.85, p<0.0001), Aβ40 Figures 5B,F (5 and 23)=104.07, p<0.0001), Aβ42+P3-26 (Figures 5C,F (5 and 23)=32.72, p<0.0001) and Aβ42 (Figures 5C,F (5 and 23)=166.2, p<0.0001) peptides were significantly increased in a sex-independent but gene-dosage-dependent manner in Apps/h and Apps/s rats as compared to Apph/h animals.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Aβ38, Aβ40+P3-24, Aβ40, Aβ42+P3-26 and Aβ42 peptides were significantly increased in a sex-independent but gene-dosage-dependent manner in Apps/h and Apps/s rats as compared to Apph/h animals.
source: While Aβ38+P3-22 levels were not significantly altered by either sex or genotype (Figures 5A,F (5 and 23)=1.779, p=0.1570), Aβ38 (Figures 5A,F (5 and 23)=27.42, p<0.0001), Aβ40+P3-24 (Figures 5B,F (5 and 23)=86.85, p<0.0001), Aβ40 Figures 5B,F (5 and 23)=104.07, p<0.0001), Aβ42+P3-26 (Figures 5C,F (5 and 23)=32.72, p<0.0001) and Aβ42 (Figures 5C,F (5 and 23)=166.2, p<0.0001) peptides were significantly increased in a sex-independent but gene-dosage-dependent manner in Apps/h and Apps/s rats as compared to Apph/h animals.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figures 5A, 5B, and 5C.

claim: No sex specific effect on Aβ/P3 peptides production was detected in Apps rats.
source: We did not detect any sex specific effect on Aβ/P3 peptides production.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The Aβ42+P3-26/Aβ40+P3-24 ratio was highest in Apph/h female rats.
source: The Aβ42+P3-26/Aβ40+P3-24 ratio was highest in Apph/h female rats (Figures 5D,F (5 and 23)=4.745, p=0.0040) while the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio was similar in all rats (Figures 5D,F (5 and 23)=1.735, p=1667).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio was similar in all Apps rats.
source: The Aβ42+P3-26/Aβ40+P3-24 ratio was highest in Apph/h female rats (Figures 5D,F (5 and 23)=4.745, p=0.0040) while the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio was similar in all rats (Figures 5D,F (5 and 23)=1.735, p=1667).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: P3 peptides may be decreased in Apps/h and Apps/s rats.
source: Even for this set of animals, the significance of the differences among genotypes is higher in 6E10 measurements as compared to 4G8 measurements, once again especially when comparing Aβ42+P3-26 and Aβ42 ELISAs- suggesting that P3 peptides may be decreased Apps/h and Apps/s rats.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the difference in significance between 6E10 and 4G8 measurements.

claim: sAPPα is significantly reduced in both Apps/h and Apps/s male rats.
source: As shown in Figure 5E (F (5, 23)=5.762, p=0.0014), sAPPα is significantly reduced in both Apps/h and Apps/s male rats.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Female Apps rats show a significant sAPPα steady-state levels reduction only in homozygous Apps/s rats.
source: Female rats show a significant sAPPα steady-state levels reduction only in homozygous Apps/s rats.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The sAPPβ produced by β-cleavage of the Swedish APP mutant differs at the COOH-terminus from the sAPPβ produced by β-cleavage of humanized APP mutant.
source: The sAPPβ produced by β-cleavage of the Swedish APP mutant -which is called sAPPβ-Sw- differs at the COOH-terminus from the sAPPβ produced by β-cleavage of humanized APP mutant -which we refer to as sAPPβ-WT- since the KM > NL mutations are in the 2 COOH-terminal residues of sAPPβ moieties.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the Swedish mutation location and its effect on sAPPβ structure.

claim: The MSD sAPPα/sAPPβ MSD ELISA kit will only recognize sAPPβ-WT.
source: Thus, the MSD sAPPα/sAPPβ MSD ELISA kit will only recognize sAPPβ-WT, as shown by the fact that this kit does not detect sAPPβ in Apps/s rats (Figure 5F, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In Apps/h rats, levels of sAPPβ-Sw are ~10 times higher than the levels of sAPPβ-WT.
source: The first striking observation is that, in Apps/h rats, levels of sAPPβ-Sw are ~10 times higher than the levels of sAPPβ-WT suggesting that in these animals, APPSw is cleaved by β-secretase at a rate 10 times higher than APPwt.
evidence: This is an inference based on ELISA data comparing sAPPβ-Sw and sAPPβ-WT levels.

claim: In Apps/h rats, APPSw is cleaved by β-secretase at a rate 10 times higher than APPwt.
source: The first striking observation is that, in Apps/h rats, levels of sAPPβ-Sw are ~10 times higher than the levels of sAPPβ-WT suggesting that in these animals, APPSw is cleaved by β-secretase at a rate 10 times higher than APPwt.
evidence: This is an inference based on ELISA data comparing sAPPβ-Sw and sAPPβ-WT levels.

claim: Total sAPPβ is significantly increased in a gene-dosage dependent manner in both sexes of Apps rats.
source: To compare the total sAPPβ steady-state levels in these rats, we added the signals detected for sAPPβ-WT to those detected for sAPPβ-Sw (Figure 5F, left panel). Total sAPPβ is significantly increased in a gene-dosage dependent manner in both sexes: in addition, male Apps/s rats had significantly higher sAPPβ-Sw levels as compared to female Apps/s rats (F (5, 23)=163.1, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Male Apps/s rats had significantly higher sAPPβ-Sw levels as compared to female Apps/s rats.
source: To compare the total sAPPβ steady-state levels in these rats, we added the signals detected for sAPPβ-WT to those detected for sAPPβ-Sw (Figure 5F, left panel). Total sAPPβ is significantly increased in a gene-dosage dependent manner in both sexes: in addition, male Apps/s rats had significantly higher sAPPβ-Sw levels as compared to female Apps/s rats (F (5, 23)=163.1, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: There was a trend towards decreased amounts of total full-length APP in Apps/s rats, which reached significance only in male Apps/s rats compared to Apph/h rats.
source: Probing against the C-terminus of APP revealed a trend towards decreased amounts of total full-length APP in Apps/s rats, which reached significance only in male Apps/s rats compared to Apph/h rats (Figure 6A, males F (2, 11)=11.08, p=0.0023; females F (2, 12)=2.987, p=0.0886).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There was no statistical difference in imAPP levels in any of the genotypes of each sex in Apps rats.
source: Separating out the glycosylated, mature form, there was no statistical difference in imAPP levels in any of the genotypes of each sex (Figure 6B, males F (2, 11)=2.125, p=0.1658; females F (2, 12)=1.516, p=0.2589), however, a significant decrease was seen in mAPP levels in Apps/s rats compared to Apph/h (Figure 6C, males F (2, 11)=15.57, p=0.0006; females F (2, 12)=5.053, p=0.0256).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A significant decrease was seen in mAPP levels in Apps/s rats compared to Apph/h.
source: Separating out the glycosylated, mature form, there was no statistical difference in imAPP levels in any of the genotypes of each sex (Figure 6B, males F (2, 11)=2.125, p=0.1658; females F (2, 12)=1.516, p=0.2589), however, a significant decrease was seen in mAPP levels in Apps/s rats compared to Apph/h (Figure 6C, males F (2, 11)=15.57, p=0.0006; females F (2, 12)=5.053, p=0.0256).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When mAPP levels are normalized to imAPP levels, the effect is only seen in Apps/s rats, with no sex differences.
source: The data suggest a trend toward a gene-dose dependent decrease in mAPP levels, but the data are not significant for all comparisons and, when mAPP levels are normalized to imAPP levels, the effect is only seen in Apps/s rats, with no sex differences (Figure 6D, males F (2, 11)=5.292, p=0.0245; females F (2, 12)=11.05, p=0.0019).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The decrease in mAPP in Apps rats is not likely the result of decreased expression of APP, but may reflect a β-processing driven depletion of the total pool of mAPP.
source: This decrease, which we also observed in a different rat cohort (Tambini et al., 2019), is not likely the result of decreased expression of APP, given that APP mRNA levels are unchanged in this model (Tambini et al., 2019), but may reflect, given the large increase in Aβ and sAPPβ-Sw production (Figure 5), a β-processing driven depletion of the total pool of mAPP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mRNA data and the increased Aβ and sAPPβ-Sw production.

claim: Previous generation of a similar App-KI mouse model of the Swedish mutation did not reveal any alteration in mAPP levels.
source: Previous generation of a similar App-KI mouse model of the Swedish mutation did not reveal any alteration in mAPP levels, though this possibility was not specifically tested (Saito et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: βCTF levels were significantly increased in Apps/s rats of both sexes.
source: βCTF levels were significantly increased in Apps/s rats of both sexes (Figure 6E, males F (2, 11)=7.926, p=0.0074; females F (2, 12)=5.819, p=0.0171).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Levels of αCTF were not significantly different in Apps rats.
source: Levels of αCTF were not significantly different (Figure 6F, males F (2, 11)=0.620, p=0.5557; females (F (2, 12)=0.732, p=0.5012).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The βCTF/αCTF ratio was increased significantly in a gene-dosage dependent manner in both sexes of Apps rats.
source: The βCTF/αCTF ratio was increased significantly in a gene-dosage dependent manner in both sexes (Figure 6G, males F (2, 11)=66.89, p<0.0001; females F (2, 12)=24.78, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The pathogenic Swedish mutation reduced the rate of APP processing by α-secretase and increased rate of APP cleavage by β-secretase in a gene-dosage dependent manner.
source: Overall, the data suggest that this pathogenic mutation reduced the rate of APP processing by α-secretase and increased rate of APP cleavage by β-secretase in a gene-dosage dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective Western blot and ELISA data from Figures 5 and 6.

claim: App Swedish rats show a significant decrease in APP in a gene-dosage dependent manner.
source: As shown in Figure 7A and B, App Swedish rats show a significant decrease in APP (females F (2, 12)=67.62, p<0.0001; males F (2, 11)=5.760, p=0.0194) and a significant increase in βCTF steady-state levels (females F (2, 12)=49.69, p<0.0001; males (F (2, 11)=28.55, p<0.0001): these changes are gene-dosage dependent.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: App Swedish rats show a significant increase in βCTF steady-state levels in a gene-dosage dependent manner.
source: As shown in Figure 7A and B, App Swedish rats show a significant decrease in APP (females F (2, 12)=67.62, p<0.0001; males F (2, 11)=5.760, p=0.0194) and a significant increase in βCTF steady-state levels (females F (2, 12)=49.69, p<0.0001; males (F (2, 11)=28.55, p<0.0001): these changes are gene-dosage dependent.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: βCTF levels are significantly reduced in female Appp/p rats.
source: Assessments of βCTF and APP levels (representative Western blots are shown in Figure 7C) showed a decrease in βCTF (Figure 7D); this decrease was significant in females (p=0.0023), trended toward significance in males (p=0.0549), and significance increased when male and female data were grouped together (p=0.0007).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: APP levels were similar in Apph/h and Appp/p animals.
source: In contrast, APP levels were similar in Apph/h and Appp/p animals (Figure 7E, females p=0.2123; males p=0.4846; females + males p=0.1810).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: βCTF levels are significantly reduced in female Appp/p rats when measured as βCTF/APP, βCTF/GAPDH, and βCTF/Ponc ratios.
source: All 3 analyses indicate that βCTF levels are significantly reduced in female Appp/p rats (Figure 7F, p<0.0001; Figure 7G, p=0.0002; Figure 7H, p=0.0083).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figures 7F, 7G, and 7H.

claim: The reduction in βCTF in male Appp/p rats was significant for the βCTF/APP and βCTF/GAPDH ratios and trended toward significance for the βCTF/Ponc ratio.
source: As for the males, the reduction in βCTF in Appp/p rats was significant for the βCTF/APP and βCTF/GAPDH ratios and trended toward significance for the βCTF/Ponc ratio (Figure 7F, p=0.0257; Figure 7G, p=0.0059; Figure 7H, p=0.0877).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figures 7F, 7G, and 7H.

claim: The differences in βCTF levels were more obvious in female rats.
source: The differences in βCTF levels were more obvious in female rats.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the data between male and female rats.

claim: Biochemical studies have identified that the Swedish and protective mutations result in increased and decreased affinity, respectively, of APP for BACE1.
source: Biochemical studies have identified that the Swedish and protective mutations result in increased and decreased affinity, respectively, of APP for BACE1.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior biochemical studies.

claim: APP and βCTF form homotypic dimers.
source: It has also been reported that APP and βCTF form homotypic dimers (Scheuermann et al., 2001; Winkler et al., 2015), therefore it is conceivable that APPSw and APPp might interact in such a way that the effect of each mutation may be abrogated or partially abrogated by the other mutant allele.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Aβ38, Aβ40+P3-24, Aβ40, Aβ42+P3-26 and Aβ42 peptides were significantly increased in a sex-independent but Swedish allele dosage-dependent manner in Apps/h and Apps/p rats as compared to Apph/h and Appp/h rats.
source: While Aβ38+P3-22 levels were not significantly altered by either gender sex or genotype (Figures 8A,F (7 and 32)=0.8586, p=0.5488), Aβ38 (Figures 8A,F (7 and 32)=7.310, p<0.0001), Aβ40+P3-24 (Figures 8B,F (7 and 32)=107.2, p<0.0001), Aβ40 (Figures 8B,F (7 and 32)=92.87, p<0.0001), Aβ42+P3-26 (Figures 8C,F (7 and 32)=42.82, p<0.0001) and Aβ42 (Figures 8C,F (7 and 32)=57.57, p<0.0001) peptides were significantly increased in a sex-independent but Swedish allele dosage-dependent manner in Apps/h and Apps/p rats as compared to Apph/h and Appp/h rats (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figures 8A, 8B, and 8C.

claim: There is a trend toward a decrease in amyloid production in Apps/p compared to Apps/h rats.
source: In general, there is a trend toward a decrease in amyloid production in Apps/p compared to Apps/h rats, however, the magnitude of the decrease is on the same order of magnitude as the decrease in amyloid production between Apph/h and Appp/h rats, which would argue against allelic interaction.
evidence: This is an observation from the ELISA data.

claim: The magnitude of the decrease in amyloid production in Apps/p compared to Apps/h rats is on the same order of magnitude as the decrease in amyloid production between Apph/h and Appp/h rats, which would argue against allelic interaction.
source: In general, there is a trend toward a decrease in amyloid production in Apps/p compared to Apps/h rats, however, the magnitude of the decrease is on the same order of magnitude as the decrease in amyloid production between Apph/h and Appp/h rats, which would argue against allelic interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the magnitudes of changes in amyloid production.

claim: The Aβ42+P3-26/Aβ40+P24 ratio was highest in Appp/h female rats and male Apps/h rats.
source: The Aβ42+P3-26/Aβ40+P24 ratio was highest in Appp/h female rats and male Apps/h rats (Figures 8D,F (7 and 32)=6.875, p<0.0001), though when P3 is not considered, the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio similar in all rats (Figures 8D,F (7 and 32)=2.152, p=0.0661).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: When P3 is not considered, the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio is similar in all rats.
source: The Aβ42+P3-26/Aβ40+P24 ratio was highest in Appp/h female rats and male Apps/h rats (Figures 8D,F (7 and 32)=6.875, p<0.0001), though when P3 is not considered, the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio similar in all rats (Figures 8D,F (7 and 32)=2.152, p=0.0661).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The protective mutation in heterozygosity does not lead to a significant increase in sAPPα levels in the Apps/p cohort.
source: In opposition to the data presented in Figure 3E, in this set of samples the protective mutation in heterozygosity does not lead to a significant increase in sAPPα levels (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The presence of a Swedish allele resulted in a decrease in sAPPα, significantly in males and only as a trend in females.
source: The presence of a Swedish allele resulted in a decrease in sAPPα, significantly in males and only as a trend in females (Figures 8E,F (7 and 32)=4.657, p<0.0011), and a significant increase in sAPPβ-Sw (Figures 8F,F (7 and 32)=163.1, p<0.0001) for both sexes.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The presence of a Swedish allele resulted in a significant increase in sAPPβ-Sw for both sexes.
source: The presence of a Swedish allele resulted in a decrease in sAPPα, significantly in males and only as a trend in females (Figures 8E,F (7 and 32)=4.657, p<0.0011), and a significant increase in sAPPβ-Sw (Figures 8F,F (7 and 32)=163.1, p<0.0001) for both sexes.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Female rats show a significant increase in sAPPβ-Sw in Apps/p compared to Apps/h.
source: Unexpectedly, female rats show a significant increase in sAPPβ-Sw in Apps/p compared to Apps/h, which might suggest some degree of allele interaction, though it is unclear how valid this finding is as this decrease is not reflected in Aβ levels, where the opposite trend is seen.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data, though the authors express uncertainty about its validity.

claim: The effect of the Swedish and protective mutations on APP-processing occur independently, and the magnitude of the increase in β-processing of APP caused by the Swedish mutation is not abrogated by the presence of a protective allele.
source: Overall, the data argue that the effect of the Swedish and protective mutations on APP-processing occur independently, and the magnitude of the increase in β-processing of APP caused by the Swedish mutation is not abrogated by the presence of a protective allele.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective ELISA data from Figure 8.

claim: There is no significant difference with regard to levels of Aβ40, Aβ42, sAPPα and sAPPβ between real and hypothetical Apps/p rats.
source: There is no significant difference with regard to levels of Aβ40 (Figures 9A,F (4 and 45)=187.6, p<0.0001), Aβ42 (Figures 9B,F (4 and 45)=113.3, p<0.0001), sAPPα (Figures 9C,F (4 and 45)=9.893, p<0.0001) and sAPPβ (Figures 9D,F (4 and 45)=76.86, p<0.0001) between real and hypothetical Apps/p rats, which is consistent with the idea that each allele's effect on APP metabolism is independent and additive.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of real and calculated ELISA data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Each allele's effect on APP metabolism is independent and additive.
source: There is no significant difference with regard to levels of Aβ40 (Figures 9A,F (4 and 45)=187.6, p<0.0001), Aβ42 (Figures 9B,F (4 and 45)=113.3, p<0.0001), sAPPα (Figures 9C,F (4 and 45)=9.893, p<0.0001) and sAPPβ (Figures 9D,F (4 and 45)=76.86, p<0.0001) between real and hypothetical Apps/p rats, which is consistent with the idea that each allele's effect on APP metabolism is independent and additive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of real and calculated ELISA data.

claim: Total APP levels and mAPP are significantly lower in female Apps/p rats.
source: Total APP levels (Figure 10A, males F (3, 16)=1.725, p=0.2022; females F (3, 16)=6.525, p=0.0043) and mAPP (Figure 10C, males F (3, 16)=2.794, p=0.0739; females F (3, 16)=7.551, p=0.0023), but not imAPP (Figure 10B, males F (3, 16)=0.5694 P=0.6432; females F (3, 16)=3.194, p=0.0520), are significantly lower in female Apps/p rats.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figures 10A and 10C.

claim: imAPP levels are not significantly different in Apps/p rats.
source: Total APP levels (Figure 10A, males F (3, 16)=1.725, p=0.2022; females F (3, 16)=6.525, p=0.0043) and mAPP (Figure 10C, males F (3, 16)=2.794, p=0.0739; females F (3, 16)=7.551, p=0.0023), but not imAPP (Figure 10B, males F (3, 16)=0.5694 P=0.6432; females F (3, 16)=3.194, p=0.0520), are significantly lower in female Apps/p rats.
